source: Ngai & Gilbert (2026) Metacognitive training facilitates optimal cognitive offloading
finding: Brief metacognitive training (5 trials: predict memory, then get true feedback) made reminder use more optimal. Predictions alone did not work.
numbers: Exp1 N=164: absolute reminder bias lower with feedback, t(161.4)=-1.67, p=.048 one-tailed, d=0.26. Exp2 N=416 replicated: full intervention vs control d=0.26; prediction-only not significant; performance feedback vs control d=0.35, p=.006. Hindsight bias d=.36.
limits: Pre-registered but one-tailed tests; small effects; pay tied to optimal choice; earlier feedback studies found no change in offloading.
agent_relevance: Show the agent its true per-tool error rate instead of asking it to guess. Route to code when the measured error is above a threshold.

source: Gilbert et al. (2020) optimal offloading paradigm, as summarised in Ngai & Gilbert (2026)
finding: People over-use reminders even when internal memory pays more. The bias is stable within a person. Confidence drives reminder setting, even when confidence is manipulated and accuracy is not.
numbers: Cited: Gilbert 2020, Ball 2022, Froscher 2022, Kirk 2021, Sachdeva & Gilbert 2020/2024 all find excess reminder use. Gilbert 2020 Exp3: feedback valence x practice difficulty shifted confidence and reminder use with no change in true memory. Reminders cut memory errors by an order of magnitude or more.
limits: Read as cited in a 2026 paper, not the PNAS original.
agent_relevance: Decide to offload from a measured error rate, not from the model's stated confidence, which is biased and movable.

source: Grinschgl et al. (2020, 2025) feedback studies, as cited in Ngai & Gilbert (2026)
finding: Fake feedback changed working-memory confidence but not offloading in the Pattern Copy Task. A single feedback statement in 2025 did not improve metacognitive judgements.
numbers: Cited results only: confidence changed, offloading unchanged (2020); no improvement in metacognitive judgement on three measures (2025).
limits: Second-hand. Differences from the successful study: fake vs true feedback, no pay tied to optimality.
agent_relevance: Changing the belief does not always change the behaviour. Use a code rule, not a request to be careful.

source: Grinschgl, Papenmeier & Meyerhoff (2021) Consequences of cognitive offloading: Boosting performance but diminishing memory
finding: Easier offloading gave faster performance but worse memory for the offloaded items.
numbers: Three experiments, N=172 each (Pattern Copy Task). Exp1: no-lockout (more offloading) faster, t(170)=-3.31, p=.001; worse memory: identity t(170)=-2.76, p=.006, np2=.04; identity-location bindings 5.91 vs 7.07 of 12.
limits: Lab task with screen images; effect sizes small (np2 about .04).
agent_relevance: State kept in code is not held in the agent's context. Fine when only the result is needed; surface values back into context when later steps must reason on them.

source: Grinschgl et al. (2021) Exp 3 boundary condition
finding: Offloading is not harmful to memory in every case. With an explicit learning goal the harm is mostly removed.
numbers: Exp2 (N=172): offloading stayed harmful even when aware of the test. Exp3 (N=172): participants forced to offload maximally but aware of the memory test almost fully counteracted the cost.
limits: Same task and sample; no independent replication opened.
agent_relevance: Pair offloading with an explicit recap or read-back step when the value is needed later.

source: Photo-taking impairment replication, Psychon Bull Rev (2022): Does taking multiple photos lead to a photo-taking-impairment effect?
finding: Photo-taking impairs memory for paintings, also between subjects, with five photos, and when photos would not be available at test.
numbers: 3 experiments, 30 paintings. Combined fixed-effects: Observe vs 5-Photo d=0.62 [0.40,0.84]; Observe vs 1-Photo d=0.35 [0.14,0.57]; 1-Photo vs 5-Photo d=0.26 [0.05,0.47]. Exp3 groups about 80 (84 in 1-Photo, 78 in 5-Photo).
limits: Undergraduates, screen paintings. Impairment persisted when photos were unavailable, which weakens a pure offloading account in favour of attentional disengagement.
agent_relevance: More saves did not buy more memory. Offload without disengaging from content the agent still needs to reason about.

source: Henkel (2014) Point-and-shoot memories, as cited in the 2022 replication
finding: Original photo-taking impairment. Zooming in on a feature attenuated the impairment for all features of zoomed objects.
numbers: Museum tour study; numbers not read.
limits: Second-hand summary.
agent_relevance: Active engagement with content (select the key part) protects memory; a passive save does not.

source: Snap & Write: photo and note taking on lecture memory (Behav Sci 2025)
finding: Photo-taking harmed in-person lecture memory, but an Exp1 interaction failed to replicate in Exp2, and the online Exp3 found a photo-taking benefit.
numbers: Three studies. Online within-subject test: photographed on-slide content M=0.31 vs 0.26, F(1,191)=6.90, p=.009, eta2=.008; notes 0.32 vs 0.24, F(1,191)=17.06, p<.001. Overall photo effect p=.052. Mind wandering did not explain the results.
limits: Effects depend on modality and on content type; reported effect sizes are tiny.
agent_relevance: The sign of an offloading effect can flip with context. Measure on the agent's own task.

source: Boettger, Poschik & Zierer (2023) Does the Brain Drain Effect Really Exist? A Meta-Analysis
finding: Smartphone presence or use has a small negative effect on cognition, mostly memory, not attention, and differs by region.
numbers: 22 studies, 43 effects. Overall g=-0.14 [-0.24,-0.03], I2=61.8%. Memory g=-0.23; attention g=-0.07 ns; general cognition g=0.10 ns. Asia g=-0.39; Europe -0.20 ns; North America -0.03 ns. Ruiz Pardo & Minda 2022 and others report nulls.
limits: Small pooled effect, high heterogeneity, funnel plot judged by eye, mixes presence and use.
agent_relevance: The strong claim that a nearby tool drains capacity is weak. Do not design around it.

source: Sparrow, Liu & Wegner (2011) Google effects on memory, and the 2018 many-lab replication
finding: Original: people remember less of what they expect to stay saved. A 2018 social-science replication project reportedly did not reproduce it.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened, from prior knowledge. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: The headline is uncertain. The better-supported effect is narrow: less memory for exactly what was saved.

source: Storm & Stone (2015) Saving-enhanced memory
finding: Saving a file freed resources and improved memory for new material, but only when the saved item was trusted.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened, from prior knowledge. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Offloaded state frees capacity only if the store is trusted. Code state must be reliable and visible.

source: Let it go: How trusted reminders alter intention maintenance (Psychon Bull Rev 2026)
finding: At first reminders helped without lowering internal rehearsal. After reliable support, the 100% group dropped rehearsal and failed when reminders were withdrawn.
numbers: N=320; reliability 0/50/100% x present/absent; thought probes; power for f=.192, at least 135 per availability condition. Critical trials: 100% group had fewer PM thoughts and worse retrieval when reminders were withdrawn.
limits: Student sample; probes are a proxy; two preregistered experiments merged.
agent_relevance: A reliable store lets the agent stop tracking, as intended. The risk is a silent store failure. Verify the store is present.

source: Between Alarms and Scheduling: cognitive offloading and prospective vs retrospective memory (Behav Sci 2026)
finding: Alarms and auto-sent emails raised on-time action a lot but did not change recall of a video.
limits: 48 hour delay, one task, students.
agent_relevance: Offloading is very effective for do-X-at-time-T and for counts. No memory cost for unrelated content here.

source: Strategic reminder setting for time-based intentions (Mem Cognit 2025)
finding: Reminders improved accuracy. People set more at longer delays, driven partly by belief about need, not real need. An always-visible clock reduced offloading.
numbers: Two-back ongoing task; delays 10, 20, 30 s. Clock experiment: 96 kept of 144 tested (48 per group). Another sample of 52 (33 men, 19 women).
limits: Lab timing task; high exclusion rates.
agent_relevance: Free always-visible state (counter, clock) reduces the need to offload. Show the counter to the model each step.

source: Get the unbalance right: asymmetric transfer effects in cognitive offloading (Cogn Res Princ Implic 2026)
finding: Removing an offloading aid hurt more than adding one helped.
numbers: Exp1 group x block F(3,132)=8.42, p<.001, np2=.16 on route deviation; pen->no-pen groups planned longer routes when the aid was gone, t(132)=2.99, p=.003, d=.52. Exp2 added visual aids.
limits: One planning task; strategy-switch cost is the proposed cause, not tested against rivals.
agent_relevance: Keep tool availability the same in development and deployment. Do not tune prompts with a tool and ship without it.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL: Program-aided Language Models
finding: The model writes code, an interpreter does arithmetic and counting. This beat chain-of-thought and stayed stable on large numbers.
numbers: GSM8K: PAL 72.0 vs COT PaLM-540B 56.9 (stated +15 points). GSM-HARD: COT fell from 65.6 to 20.1, PAL held 61.5. Object counting PAL 96.7 vs COT +23.7 points. Repeat copy +21.8 over COT.
limits: Codex-era models; table extract garbled so some pairings come from the prose.
agent_relevance: Direct support for keeping counts and arithmetic in code.

source: Gao et al. (2022) PAL error analysis
finding: Most chain-of-thought failures on big-number problems are arithmetic slips, not wrong reasoning.
numbers: 16 of 25 analysed cases had nearly identical thoughts with and without large numbers. DIRECT fell 19.7 to 5.0 on GSM-HARD (74% relative).
limits: Small manual sample of 25.
agent_relevance: Offload when the failure is computation. It will not help when the failure is understanding the problem.

source: Chen et al. (2022) Program of Thoughts Prompting
finding: Splitting reasoning (model) from computation (interpreter) beat chain-of-thought on math and finance sets.
numbers: Few-shot average gain over CoT about 8% on math word problems and 15% on financial sets; zero-shot about 12%; PoT+SC beats CoT+SC by about 10%. A CoT + calculator ablation gains more than 8 points on GSM8K, AQuA and TabMWP over plain CoT.
limits: Codex; the calculator alone recovers part of the gain.
agent_relevance: A plain calculator tool already captures much of the benefit; full program generation adds more.

source: Li et al. (2023) Chain of Code
finding: Code plus a model that simulates the non-executable lines beat code-only and thought-only. Code-only fails on non-algorithmic tasks.
numbers: BIG-Bench Hard: 84% with text-davinci-003, 91% with GPT-4; above average human raters; above best raters on algorithmic subset. Python-only fails almost all non-algorithmic tasks. Smaller models also gain, while CoT helps only the largest.
limits: BBH tasks; human raters had no code access.
agent_relevance: Offload only what can be computed; leave fuzzy parts to the model; fall back to the model if code errors.

source: Schick et al. (2023) Toolformer
finding: A GPT-J model that learned to call a calculator more than doubled math word problem scores and beat GPT-3 175B without tools.
numbers: Table 4 ASDiv/SVAMP/MAWPS: Toolformer 14.8/6.3/15.0 vs a GPT-3 175B 14.0/10.0/19.8 vs OPT 66B 6.0/4.9/7.9 in my read; the extracted table is garbled so cell assignment is uncertain. Calculator used on 97.9% of examples. Limitations: no chained tool calls, sample inefficient.
limits: Zero-shot; table read uncertain.
agent_relevance: Tool use is cheap to learn and can stand in for scale on arithmetic.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT
finding: Essay writers using an LLM could not quote their own essay and showed weaker low-frequency connectivity than search or unaided writers.
numbers: N=54 (18 per group), 3 sessions; 18 did session 4 with groups swapped. Could not quote: 15/18 (83.3%) LLM vs 2/18 (11.1%) each for search and brain-only, p<.001. Full ownership: LLM 9/18, brain-only 16/18.
limits: Preprint under review; small N; session 4 only 18; writing task, not counting.
agent_relevance: Offloading the whole thought removes recall of it. Our agent offloads state and counts, not reasoning.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Borrowed or kept? Self-generation-first vs direct-adoption AI workflows
finding: After direct adoption of AI output, unaided reasoning was worse. A self-generation-first workflow did not fall below baseline.
numbers: 900 randomised, 659 analysed. Dependent vs no-AI: -0.38 on 1-7 scale, d=-0.28, p=0.0002. Test 15-20 min later with the tool removed.
limits: Immediate near transfer only; arms differ in generation, effort and autonomy; no mechanism isolated.
agent_relevance: Order matters: commit a first attempt, then interrogate with the tool.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) Not all cognitive offloading is equal: dependent vs autonomous offloading to generative AI
finding: Delegating core thinking went with loss of agency and motivation; scaffold use went with better self-reported outcomes. Immediate benefits looked the same.
numbers: Three-wave survey, N=589 students and early-career workers. Metacognitive monitoring weakened agency transfer from dependent offloading but not the motivation link.
limits: Self-report, correlational, no performance measures.
agent_relevance: Immediate benefit cannot tell good from bad delegation. Use a held-out check.

source: Risko & Gilbert (2016) Cognitive offloading, as cited in 2026 papers
finding: Defines cognitive offloading as using body and environment to reduce cognitive demand, with benefits and costs.
numbers: Definition only, from citations.
limits: Review not opened.
agent_relevance: Offloading involves a decision of when, and a cost in effort, trust and memory.

source: Moderator summary from the opened papers
finding: Moderators seen: learning goal, trust in store, reliability, task type (action vs recall), modality (in person vs online), region, and who makes the first attempt.
numbers: Known test (Grinschgl 2021 Exp3); 100% reliable store; delay length; online photo benefit; Asia g=-0.39 vs NA -0.03; direct adoption d=-0.28.
limits: Synthesis of lines above, not a new source.
agent_relevance: Offload counts and clock; keep the model's own first attempt; make the store visible and checked.

source: Intervention summary from the opened papers
finding: Worked: predictions plus true feedback; known memory test; self-generation first. Did not work: predictions alone, fake feedback, single feedback statements.
numbers: d about .26 to .35 for feedback interventions; d=-0.28 for harm of direct adoption; no effect for prediction-only.
limits: Small effects, mostly students and online tasks.
agent_relevance: Tell the agent its measured accuracy on counting, then route counts to code.
